title: File:Grandmas Pork with rice.jpg
artist: Alpha from Melbourne, Australia
description:
The Bund's version of 红烧肉 Grandma's Pork or red-cooked pork was very good. The sauce was syrupy and fragrant, coating firm pieces of fatty belly pork. The firmness means that the fatty layer is still intact and bouncy. The belly meat also has smaller seams of fat which makes the meat moist and tender.

I wonder if this is the famous 婆婆肉 Grandma's Pork or 红烧肉 Red-Cooked Pork? It seems 红烧 red cooking is a typical Shanghai cooking style.

--- 外滩 The Bund Restaurant Level 1 / 206 Bourke St Melbourne VIC 3000 (03)96630005 www.thebundrestaurant.com.au/

title: File:Kung Pao Chicken - Jadeland Restaurant, Ottawa (6453176819).jpg
artist: John Thompson from Iqaluit
description:
Gong Bao Ji Ding at the Jadeland Restaurant, Ottawa - August 19, 2011 Appeared on the menu as 'Kung Po Chicken' in English and 宫保鸡丁 in Chinese characters.

A very poor effort for what is supposed to be a Sichuan restaurant. The chicken was sliced instead of cut into cubes despite saying '丁 ' on the menu. There were no chilli pieces and no scorched chilli taste. Cashews were used instead of peanuts. There was very little chicken and lots of vegetables used for bulk. These included diced carrot and bamboo shoot, peas, celery, baby corncob chunks and big pieces of green pepper. The chilli consisted only of very fine flecks in a mediocre sauce which was nondescript and would have been at home in a canned chop suey.

<a href="http://www.jadeland.com/" rel="nofollow">www.jadeland.com/</a>
label_source: Commons category; weak label, not individually verified

title: File:Kung Pao Chicken - Keung Kee Restaurant, Montreal (6650429089).jpg
artist: John Thompson from Iqaluit
description: This was a fairly mediocre dish but not too bad for a Cantonese restaurant, I suppose. There was not a great deal of chicken and the pieces were cut more in shreds rather than the cubes which the ‘ding’ in the Chinese name calls for. There were a lot of peanuts and, somewhat unusually, the red skins were left on and that actually added to the visual appeal of the dish. As with most restaurants, there were quite a few vegetables added for filler. In this case there were green peppers, carrot and celery, as well as some yellow onion. The sauce was quite spicy hot and I was able to discern some flakes of chill but the traditional whole chilies were not present and the dish lacked a scorched chili flavor. There was also almost no sweet-sour quality to the sauce. Cantonese restaurants quite often will make this dish far sweeter than in Sichanese versions but this was uncharacteristically flat in that regard. I liked it well enough but it rates only 3 out of 5 in my mind.
label_source: Commons category; weak label, not individually verified
